description: An application surface owes a keyboard, and owes it to be small. A dashboard is operated for twenty minutes at a stretch by somebody who already knows where everything is, and the actions worth a key are the ones where reaching for the pointer costs more than the action itself: opening a search that reaches the whole product, and changing the shape of the screen. A key that saves one click on a control already visible is a key nobody remembers, and a list of fifty is a second navigation to learn on top of the one already on screen.

gates.title: An App Surface Has A Keyboard
gates.rule: A surface a person works in rather than reads through binds keyboard shortcuts. The two that nearly always earn one are a search or command palette reaching every destination the product has, on the modifier every other application uses for it, and a toggle for the navigation rail, on the modifier every other application uses for that. A surface with no keyboard at all is one where every action costs a trip to the pointer, including the ones taken forty times an hour.

check.message: no keyboard handler found on an app surface - at minimum a search palette and a rail toggle earn one

gates.fix: Bind a small set of shortcuts. Start with the search palette and the navigation toggle, both on the platform modifier, and add a third only where it clears the same bar.

gates.title: The Set Is Three Keys Or Fewer
gates.rule: Three shortcuts across the whole surface, and a fourth has to be argued for. The failure this catches is the shortcut list written for its own sake: a digit per filter, a letter per section, a chord per panel, none of which is remembered and all of which have to be documented. Anything already sitting on screen as a control does not get a key as well.

check.message: a key per filter or per section - the control for it is already on screen, and the key is one nobody remembers

gates.fix: Delete every shortcut standing in for a control the reader can already see, and keep the ones that change where they are or what the screen looks like.

gates.title: The Keyboard Says What It Is
gates.rule: A modified shortcut is invisible until something states it, so the surface carries a list a reader can open and a visible way to open it. The list is itself the third shortcut worth having, on `?`. A set of keys with nothing that enumerates them is a set only its author knows.

check.message: modified shortcuts are bound with nothing naming them - a reader has no way to discover a chord

gates.fix: Add a shortcut list opened by `?` and by a visible control, and print the key on the control it belongs to where there is room for it.

gates.title: The Modifier Is The One The Reader Has
gates.rule: Where a key is drawn on screen it is drawn as the key that reader's own keyboard carries. A Mac shown Ctrl and a PC shown Command are each being told to press something they do not have, which is worse than printing nothing.

check.message: a modifier is printed without testing which platform is reading it

gates.fix: Pick the glyph from the platform once, and render that everywhere a key is drawn.
